text: Open-Source Intelligence, or OSINT, means gathering information from sources that are already publicly available — nothing hacked, nothing stolen. Today we'll cover the four tools a defender actually uses, why they're the exact same tools an attacker uses, and a concrete example of OSINT catching an exposed system first.

So much of an organization's footprint sits in plain sight: domain registration records, internet-wide device scans, previously leaked credentials, and what employees post publicly. Both attackers and defenders build their picture from these same public pieces. The skill isn't finding secret information — it's knowing where to look and what it adds up to.

Four tools cover most defensive OSINT. WHOIS records show who registered a domain and when. Shodan continuously scans the public internet, so a defender can search their own IP ranges and see exactly what's visible from outside. Breach databases like Have I Been Pwned flag employee credentials that have leaked. And social media review shows what employees publicly post that a social engineer could use.

Here's the part worth sitting with: every one of those tools is also exactly what an attacker uses during the Reconnaissance stage of the Cyber Kill Chain, researching a target before building a weapon. The tools are neutral. What differs is only who's looking and why — and a defender who looks first gets to fix what they find.

Picture a defender running a routine Shodan search against their own public IP range during a quarterly review. It turns up an old VPN appliance, long forgotten by IT, still reachable from the internet and running unpatched firmware. Because they found it the same way an attacker would have, they can patch it quietly, on their own schedule.

That closes out Chapter 5's threat intelligence coverage — IOCs, feeds, STIX and TAXII, and now OSINT. Chapter 6 begins next with vulnerability scanners, Nessus and OpenVAS, moving from recognizing threats to systematically finding exposure before an attacker does.
